I wish to deal further with this ex parte order. Having obtained the ex parte order, does the minister or the police have to make the details of the ex parte order public knowledge? Not on your life. The whole system can be buried. The file remains sealed until it is destroyed. The accused who is charged as a result of an improperly obtained ex parte order has no right to cross-examine the grounds on which the order was obtained in the first place. The evidence obtained against him is not open to cross-examination. The fact that it was obtained without the right to have it in the first place, without the right of being open to examination or cross-examination, is used against him.

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
Under section 178(2)(i) we find that on proof of conviction or illegal wiretapping the government of Canada, without the right to go into property and civil rights, declares a damage suit for $5,000. Surely a claim for punitive damages, which is a tort, should not be set out in the Criminal Code. After all, the Criminal Code should not set out grounds for civil damage or even limitations on grounds for civil damage. This is clearly a matter within the competence of the provinces. This section should be removed from the statute. If a person is aggrieved by the improper use of wiretapping and sues someone for that, there is no reason why the person so aggrieved should have his damages limited to $5,000 by the Parliament of Canada. The whole question of damage and civil litigation is a matter within the competence of the provinces of this country. It is not a matter of competence of the federal parliament. On that basis, this section must be removed from the statute.
There are a lot of things said by people on the telephone and otherwise. Things are sometimes said when they should not be said. Things are sometimes said in a way they should not be said. As a politician, I know that. Your Honour also knows it. Loose comments are made. Surely, loose comments made by people over the telephone and picked up as a result of the authority given to the police office to bug the telephone or otherwise should not be used as evidence in a court of law. Just because someone says he is going to do something that is possibly of a seditious nature, it should not be used in evidence against that person just because it was said in private.
This whole question must be looked at, and looked at seriously. It is very easy for politicians to talk about fixing a nomination. It is very easy for people to talk over the phone about fixing a horse race. Because it was very easy for my constituent, a middle-aged lady, to talk about getting rid of the Prime Minister, this idle chatter should not be used as evidence against her in a court of law. All of a sudden it is used against him. This is totally against our concept of British justice. On that basis, the clauses in this bill authorizing electronic snooping must be deleted.

body else has the authority to cut the season or eliminate it altogether. Therefore the bill might have included some reference to seasons.
I think we all realize that in this very large country where there is an important fishery on the west coast, a very important fishery on the east coast, and the inland fisheries, there are too many details with respect to licensing and seasons for one minister to give them all his personal attention. In essence, I suppose this is an argument in favour of the bill.
If the minister undertakes licensing, as the present act says, at his "absolute discretion" he must rely on his own department; therefore he would rely on the regional office which has responsibility for the waters in question. I have had some experience with the Atlantic regional office in Halifax and I must say I would hate to leave the matter entirely in their hands. If the minister is unable personally to oversee these matters, then automatically it devolves upon him to look to his regional offices for advice on licensing and seasons.
I have given one example of where the regional office in Halifax cut the salmon season practically in half, apparently without any reference to the minister or to anyone else. I could give another example, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, in commenting on the bill before us I should like to address my remarks in particular to clause 9 to which my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Howard) was referring a while ago. If I might make a suggestion in all humility to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), it would be that he consider looking at Bill C-165. My humility is, of course, increased as I note that this particular bill relates closely to a private member's bill submitted by myself for the consideration of the House. It is entitled "an act respecting the protection of endangered species." The material in that bill certainly relates closely to clause 9 of the bill we are presently studying. For the interest of the House I shall read the brief clause 9 of the bill before us. It is entitled "Endangered wildlife" and provides:
May 9, 1973

The minister may, in co-operation with one or more provincial governments having an interest therein, take such measures as he deems necessary for the protection of any species of non-domestic animal in danger of extinction.
I humbly submit, Mr. Speaker, that although the intention and the spirit of the clause are good, the clause is still a relatively weak one. As the expression often goes in this House, it is a provision without teeth. The only teeth that this provision would have are to be found in the mouths of the poor animals who are supposed to be protected. There are no specific provisions as to how action is to be taken. There is nothing in the clause about sanctions and there is, indeed, very little definition.
As a suggestion to the minister and to the committee I should like to put forward some distinctions and definitions which are contained in Bill C-165 which I think are more specific and useful. There is an attempt to define "endangered species" in this way:
-"endangered species" means any wild mammal, wild bird, amphibian or reptile which by regulation is declared by the minister to be threatened with extinction-
Further on there is a definition of that last phrase, "threatened with extinction":
-"threatened with extinction" means a species or subspecies which is either unlikely to continue to survive without special protective measures-
I think this underlines the point that the hon. member for Skeena was making so effectively.
-or occurs in such small numbers and/or in such a restricted or specialized habitat that it could easily disappear.
In other words, this kind of definition is, I think, more useful than the very general statement that is contained in the present bill and I think meets the kind of concern expressed by the hon. member for Skeena. However, it is not enough for us in Canada to think only of the wildlife of this country as isolated from the rest of the world. In this case as in so many others we must have an international approach to the concern we feel. It may be that practices followed in this country can have a nefarious effect on wildlife in other countries. In order to make my point 1 should like to read from an article that appeared in one of our daily newspapers this winter, from a United Press source. It is brief and reads as follows:
U.S. Attorney Robert Morse and Assistant Secretary of the Interior Nathaniel Reed said yesterday in Brooklyn federal court the largest ring of traffickers in illegal animal pelts ever uncovered had been smashed.
You might ask, quite rightly, Mr. Speaker, what are illegal animal pelts? How would we define them as being illegal in this country? I suggest it would be difficult since we do not have a law in this country that defines trafficking in certain animal pelts as illegal. The article continues:
A major company which admitted $5 million worth of purchases and sales of threatened species, including ocelot, otter, leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma, faces a $500,000 fine.
That is a fairly stiff fine. But the next paragraph is the one that should really startle us:
Reed-

-said these illegal pelts are shipped to storehouses in Canada and

Switzerland because these countries do not now prevent the purchase and sale of these skins.

reductions which will increase take-home pay and moderate the cost of a wide range of consumer products, and will at the same time provide special relief for the elderly, the veterans and their families. I defy the Prime Minister, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), the Minister of Supply and Services and, indeed, any member of the government to show the House one major corporation in the past 50 years of the history of this country that has been sold at half its book value.

Mr. Speaker, may I begin by referring to this motion and the comments of the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) because he was the most recent speaker. I would say that there are really three elements involved in this motion. The first is that there is regret expressed by the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), that we are going to change the present cost-sharing arrangements in respect of the medicare and the hospital care program.
I can understand his concern in respect of that matter, because they have been very successful programs, but at the same time I hope all hon. members will bear in mind that the motivation is only to bring forward suggestions for change in the cost-sharing arrangements and in the formulae in regard to these two programs. The motivation for change is brought about primarily because of a series of federal-provincial conferences on this subject which have taken place over the last 30 months. Constant attention has been brought to bear on this subject by the provinces and by the federal government, and there is a wide degree of unanimity in respect of the need to adjust the formulae to allow the provinces to have an input in terms of their own priority in respect of health care services.
It is very important to underline the fact that in the present arrangements the provincial governments are forced almost by necessity-because we share on a 50-50 basis-to spend more money in the area which is most expensive, such as hospital acute care beds, and so on. In other areas where they want to enter into extended services for ambulatory care and other types of preventive medicine, we do not have arrangements to allow them to do this. It is in response to their request that we are trying to make the program more flexible.

May 11, 1973
Health Care
There are a number of ways in which we can approach this question, and clearly people will make different value judgments in respect of it. One is to widen the base of the kind of services that would be eligible under these two programs, or to change the programs themselves so that they become flexible and not tied to a specific type of medical service. Federal-provincial conferences have emphasized the need to do this, and this new formula is an attempt to allow the provinces the kind of flexibility that will give them an opportunity to put more emphasis on various important areas of health care service within their borders. That is really the reason we are bringing forward the formula. It is certainly not being brought forward because we want to vacate the field. There is no intention to do that at all but, rather, to recognize that in our federal system the provincial governments have legitimate concerns in respect of their own priorities. We should respect that principle as much as we can.
However, the federal government is determined, at the same time, that we maintain certain national standards and those national standards would have to prevail whether or not there was a change in the formula. I am referring to standards such as the comprehensiveness of the programs, universality, portability in Canada and accessibility to people regardless of whether they can afford to pay for these services. Those elements must be maintained. I feel that although there is a proposal to change the formula, it is a step forward, not backward. It is a step in the direction, not of balkanizing the country-which was suggested by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands-but to keep the country together because of the insistence on these national standards which would make sure that Canadians from coast to coast were treated in an equal way.

Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 41(2) I should like to lay on the table copies in both official languages of a document entitled "Mineral Policy Objectives for Canada".
A number of meetings have been held between the ministers responsible at the federal and provincial levels for mineral policy, culminating in a meeting in Ottawa on April 13 at which two decisions were concluded with respect to mineral policy in Canada.
The first of these has been the decision to set up a formal consultative and co-ordination mechanism in order to achieve more effective co-ordination in mineral policy development. Such a mechanism is essential for the formulation of mineral policies which are national in scope.
While noting that differences among governments on mineral policy matters remain, the ministers agreed that the real significance of their discussions is the beginning of new relationships among governments in the formulation of mineral policy for Canadians.
The meeting also reached agreement on the publication of a document entitled "Mineral Policy Objectives for Canada", which I am tabling today.
The document contains a more detailed description of the goal and objectives for mineral policies outlined in April, and is intended to form a background for further discussions by ministers. While this document relates to most minerals, it does not apply to fossil fuels. These, along with other energy commodities, will be the subject of extensive scrutiny within the context of papers reviewing Canada's energy policies which I will present to parliament in the near future.
Within the context of closer co-operation which is sought at the governmental level, governments must take into account each other's jurisdiction in the translation of objectives into policies. The document is not intended to state or identify policies by which any government would achieve such objectives, nor does it attempt to define or specify the particular role of any one government. However, it is a first phase in the process of intergovernmental co-operation for arriving at a mineral policy for Canada. None the less, governments will choose from a wide variety of strategies, programs, methods and techniques to achieve their objectives. References in the document tabled to possible strategies are therefore included only by way of example.
The publication of this document should be seen as a first step toward the formulation and implementation of comprehensive mineral policies for Canada.
The nation's mineral endowment can support an expanding level of output and thereby continue to contribute substantially to the economic and material well-being of future generations.
However, Canada does not have a monopoly on minerals. Indeed, Canada faces major challenges to maintain an internationally competitive sector because of increasing competition from other resource-producing nations and the efforts of larger industrial nations to secure greater long-term advantage from resource exporters.
Ministers want to explore how mineral development for both domestic needs and exports can be best undertaken to optimize long-term contribution to development throughout Canada. Such development must be sensitive to long-term economic needs, undesirable environmental impacts, the viability of communities dependent on mineral production and fabrication and more precise delineation of the long-term economic potential of our mineral endowment and the ways it can be utilized.

Consequently, it is my intention to make my remarks brief and of a general nature only. It is my opinion, having discussed the question of capital punishment over the years and listening to the speeches made in this House, that it is virtually impossible to convert a confirmed abolitionist into a retentionist or to convert a confirmed retentionist into an abolitionist. Both have arguments to support their views, both are sincere and both are able to adduce statistics to support their arguments.
Bill C-2 which we are debating today has the effect of placing a moratorium on the death penalty for a further

May 22, 1973

period of five years except as it relates to the murder of police officers and prison guards or officials. We are being asked to extend the ban after a five-year trial period because, in the words of the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand), the government does not have the full data for the whole of the previous five years. He said in the debate in this House on January 26, as reported at page 688 of Hansard:
Statistics are some two years behind and therefore at the moment we are only in possession of full data covering the first three years of the trial period.
I find that statement hard to accept in this age of computers. Surely the government, being aware of the fact that there was need to deal with this matter on or before December 30, 1972, could have given top priority to the compilation of statistics in order to have the information available to this House. But supposing we did have the statistics, Mr. Speaker-what would they prove? I suggest they would prove nothing, because since 1962 no person has been hanged in Canada. In effect, there has been no capital punishment in Canada since 1962. Since 1968 there have been four convictions for the murder of police officers and the government has commuted their death sentences.
After listening to the remarks of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in this House on January 30 last, I can appreciate the heavy responsibility that is placed upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of his cabinet when faced with the decision of whether or not a sentence of death should be commuted. But I find it hard to believe that the circumstances surrounding all murders since 1962 have warranted commutation.
There is great concern amongst responsible citizens in Canada as to the direction in which our society is going. They are concerned about the safety of their families, and well they should be under present circumstances where bail procedures are such that potentially dangerous criminals are allowed out on bail to commit further crimes, where weekend passes from prison are almost a right rather than a privilege, and where prison breaks in Canada are almost a weekly occurrence.
It is the responsibility of the government and of this House to take steps to make certain that society is protected and that citizens are able to live without fear of violence. How does a government assume this responsibility? Mr. Speaker, it assumes it by passing the legislation which makes certain that we have law and order in our country, laws which provide the rules by which we live and penalties that are punitive in nature and will deter an individual from breaking the law.
It is a further responsibility of a government to see to it that the law is enforced and that the sentences handed down by the courts are carried out. The extent of the punishment depends upon the seriousness of the crime. There is no point in having the same punishment for robbing a parking meter of a few dollars as there is for robbing a bank at gun point of $10,000. Therefore, we must have punishment which fits the crime in that the punishment must be of such a nature that it will act as a deterrent.
Capital Punishment
There is no greater crime than the taking of another's life. It has long been recognized, however, where a person was insane at the time of commission of the crime and did not know the nature and consequences of his act, that he was not guilty of murder. It has been recognized that killing in self-defence is not murder. It has been further recognized that people, being human and having emotions, at times due to aggravation, are unable to control their emotions and kill one another. This is not necessarily murder, depending upon the degree of aggravation.
Mr. Speaker, in instances where someone deliberately and with premeditation kills another, that is murder. It is also murder when a person kills someone in the commission of a crime, for in these instances he knows what he is doing and must be held accountable. If he is prepared to knowingly assume the risk, he must also assume the consequences if we are to have law and order.
In my opinion, there is no distinction between the killing of a policeman or a prison official or the killing of a private citizen. It is a life of an individual, not the life of a person in a particular occupation that is important. It is my opinion that capital punishment should be extended to those persons who kidnap another and hold them for ransom in fear of their lives, or those persons who hijack an aircraft and endanger the lives of the passengers. This, Mr. Speaker, is the stand I took throughout the election campaign and a conviction I have held for a number of years. It is not based on any poll that I took of my constituents, or on public opinion.

Adjournment Debate

This issue arose when the Auditor General reported to Parliament in 1969 that a Crown corporation for which he was the auditor, namely the CBC, failed to remit income tax arid social security to the United States government for 17 of its employees while stationed in the United States. I realize there was a period during which the CBC was not sure whether the employees fell under Canadian income tax laws or United States income tax laws. During the period in which the CBC was trying to settle this dispute it continued to make deductions from its United States-based employees at the same rates as Canadian income tax, and kept this money in trust; then for some reason or other it was later returned in the same year, 1965.
The total amount of income tax owing by these 17 people was $134,573.99. One of the employees in the group had an indebtedness of $15,000, which is included in the figure I have just mentioned. Realizing the complexity and seriousness of this whole problem, the public accounts committee appointed a subcommittee chaired by the very capable and distinguished Liberal member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik). It held six meetings, and the public accounts committee held 15 meetings to discuss this whole matter.
Witnesses from the CBC and from the Department of National Revenue were heard as well as many others, including Mr. J. A. Coates, legal counsel from an outstanding international taxation firm in Toronto, who gave evidence for the guidance of the committee. The committee reported its findings and made a 13-point report to the House. I wish time permitted me to place the whole report
[Mr. Madill.)
on the record. However, I shall mention only two recommendations. First, recommendation No. 7 reads:
That the corporation's action in 1965 was seriously inadequate in terms of taking steps to avoid exposing itself to a corporate liability without having made provision to recover the funds from its employees.
The last, and most important, recommendation made by the committee was that the CBC should immediately take steps to attempt to recover the $134,573.99 from the 17 employees involved. This matter now rests at that point. I should simply like to ask the minister the following questions, and I am sorry he is not here. First, was it not a reasonable assumption for the 17 employees of the CBC to assume that they should pay income tax in one country or the other? No one in their income bracket should be exempt. Second, I should like to ask the minister whether he feels that the hard-earned dollars of John Q. Public should be used to pay the income tax of the employees of the CBC, especially the one who had a tax liability of $15,000.
Further, I should like to ask, on what basis can a Crown corporation to whom parliament grants estimates to the tune of $200 million defy or disregard a recommendation tabled by an all-party committee of this House? Next, I should like to ask why the registered letter of March 29, 1973, was sent by the CBC to the 17 employees when it did not demand payment by the recipients. Finally, I should like to ask the minister this important question: Does he intend to instruct the CBC to collect this income tax, as recommended by an all-party committee of parliament, or does he intend to accept the refusal of the president to collect the income tax? That is the issue. It is a very important issue and one which must be settled.
I cannot understand how the president of the CBC can be taking a stand which defies a recommendation made by an all-party committee of this House. That is the issue. I hope the minister will answer these questions. I am sorry he did not feel that this was an important enough subject for thim to be here tonight to answer these questions.

I am against a hybrid situation. The Leader of the New Democratic Party never once mentioned the distinction between capital and non-capital crimes. The debate we had in 1961 was the culmination of much anxiety and soul searching on the part of members of the House in putting into the law provision for capital and non-capital murder. Very few members have mentioned this distinction between capital murder and non-capital murder, and it is only in the popular definition of capital murder that you invoke the supreme penalty. I fully appreciate that the fact that we have capital murder and non-capital murder leads to a hybrid situation, but I think members of the House are prepared to face that fact, as the Prime Minister suggested. It is a question of whether they want the law of 1961 or whether they want to vote for full abolition of capital punishment.
I interpret the present bill as providing a qualified abolition or a qualified retention. The bill still recognizes capital punishment, but its imposition, is limited to the murderers of policemen and prison guards. I appreciate the intervention of the Solicitor General, but what I am saying is that I would have followed with more conviction the premise of the Prime Minister regarding members facing their responsibility, rather than trying to hide under a sham bill which can be interpreted as providing for either abolition or for retention.

prepared to face the question squarely? I agree with the Prime Minister that the question posed in this bill is eternal. But we do not need another five year trial period. That this House, re-affirming that generations of peoples of diverse races and many nationalities have joined in peace and war to build a free Canada and to mold a Canadian nationality, regrets the government's reluctant and token recognition of this reality.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased with the opportunity to use one of our opposition days to discuss the question of multiculturalism. The diversity of origins, customs, religions, languages, literature, music and the arts is a precious Canadian asset. Retention and enhancement of these contributions to our society should be given every reasonable assistance, and where assistance involves the use of public funds it is incumbent upon the government to insure that there is no suggestion that such funds are being used to gain political favour.
To date, steps taken to implement a multicultural policy in this country have not convinced many Canadians that the aim has not been in some ways partisan. The program so far has been almost exclusively related to a few grants for this and for that; throw in a four-page ad which has the distinct appearance of election campaign material, and one could easily become suspicious of the motives. I am not being critical of the idea of grants, but it is clear that in order to realize the aims of a policy of multiculturalism much more than a few government handouts is necessary. There has to be a genuine effort to introduce appropriate legislative changes designed to give complete equality to all ethnic groups in the country.
We recognize that you cannot buy or legislate cultural activity or harmony. The government's cultural role has to be a supportive one to create the proper atmosphere and institutional basis to allow the realization by all Canadians of their cultural aspirations, and conditions must be such that these aspirations could emanate from the people, not from the state.
Multiculturalism is a uniquely Canadian concept and represents the traditional difference between the American melting pot and Canadian mosaic. This mosaic probably remains the single most important strand in the fabric of our national identity. Inside the melting pot everyone is rootless, floating like driftwood in the ocean, no roots to attach it to firm soil. Here in Canada, the English, the French and other Canadians of European origin, the Indians, are maintaining their identity and therefore maintaining their roots on Canadian soil. These groups occupy a special place in the unofficial agreement between people of various backgrounds living together, recognizing and appreciating each other's differences and respecting these while maintaining their own particular identities.
The original "B and B" concept failed to recognize this Canadian reality and in fact implied a quiet suppression of non-official cultures and languages, creating a feeling

not conducive to unity in the country. Acceptance of and recognition of Canada's multicultural reality gives official status to the positive value of the contribution of other cultures to the Canadian cultural framework. In short, Canada's basic fibre consists of many groups, each of which has a rich and cohesive internal life, each of which has a desire to reach outward, to co-operate with, and appreciate the others.
Official recognition of this Canadian multicultural reality is a new thing for many Canadians. Many Canadians have greeted this recognition with joy, while others have greeted it with some suspicion. There have been feelings expressed that in some way an official policy of multiculturalism will detract from, or undermine, Canada's two largest ethnic groups, namely the English and French.
Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize that I do not see multiculturalism in that kind of light. Multiculturalism simply adds to the richness contributed to this country by the two largest ethnic groups.

Since the passage of the Official Languages Act I believe it has become quite clear that the government has hoped to characterize probably all Canadians
June 4, 1973

into two basic groups in so far as attitude toward bilingualism is concerned. The first category is composed of all those who agree with every single thing this government has done in connection with the implementation of the bilingual program. It is composed of thousands and thousands of people across the land who have never quarrelled with the principles of bilingualism but who have been shocked and utterly appalled at the methods used by this government to institute its bilingual program. This third group is made up of Canadians who love their country too much to allow it to be torn apart by a government that has been, and is, playing politics with bilingualism and national unity, a government that gives unctuous lip service to national unity while at the same time indulging in actions and following methods that, in short, will do more to disunite this country than even avowed separatists could hope to accomplish. Mr. Speaker, the occasion for the question which I addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last May 8 on the matter of aboriginal rights arose from two separate but related events. One was the statement made to the committee on Indian affairs by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) on April 12, 1973, as recorded at page 1329 of the proceedings of the committee which reads:
The proclamation of 1763 I recognize as a valid document-It establishes on obligation for the Crown to negotiate with the natives before taking land from the Indians.
Adjournment Debate
The second event was a little later, when this House was in recess and the Prime Minister made certain public statements on television, and perhaps otherwise, among other things suggesting that the NDP was trying to rewrite history and accusing us of lack of concern for what some of the provincial governments of Canada are doing in this area. This was sufficient cause for me to ask the Prime Minister whether the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development when he was speaking before the committee was stating government policy or not. While there were certain procedural difficulties to the question as I posed it, that essentially was the question I asked and on which I would like information. The Prime Minister in his reply said it was "a very difficult legal question which I am not able to settle in any final way by any answer or, indeed, by a statement of policy."
When the Prime Minister of this country, in this day and age, was so vague about it, I felt the answer was far from being satisfactory and that I should pursue the matter further on an occasion such as this. The nub of the question that arises in my mind is why the Prime Minister continues to deal with this matter as an abstract legal question rather than as a basic human question involving basic human rights. That is the point of view from which I would like to see the question treated. Incidentally, I say at once, Mr. Speaker, that if we can get a real statement of policy, in depth from that point of view, from the government of Canada then so far as I am concerned I am quite prepared to play my part with any provincial government in this country, regardless of its political stripe, in having that government recognize its appropriate responsibility in the consideration of this matter. But until there is forthcoming from the Government of Canada a clear-cut statement of its policy, it ill behooves the Prime Minister or anyone else to criticize the position being taken in this context by provincial administrations.
There are a couple of points I would like to mention in the few minutes available to me. One arises out of the further statement by the minister on April 12 when, in reference to the B.C. land question, he said:
In the B.C. land question the judges did not agree, they split. Three judges said that the proclamation of 1763 did not apply to B.C. because B.C. was terra incognita in 1763.
My response to that is again to say, let us get it out of the legal context. The fact is, and the records indicate it, that whether or not this legally applied, certainly the first Governor and the Colonial Secretary in London at that time acted as if it did apply. The documentary evidence on that point is quite clear, if one looks afield one can pick up that kind of factual recognition almost anywhere.
I have in my hand a copy of a book just published, "Barkley Sound-A History of the Pacific Rim National Park Area," by R. Mr. Banfield in his rather voluminous reports to the Colonial Secretary at Government House, Victoria, a man named W. A. G. Young, had many interesting things to say. I was almost compelled to do so on my first coming among them; they were particularly anxious that I should purchase the ground on which I lived... saying that the Americans at Cape Flattery had all bought their ground from the Indians. I pleaded poverty, which was very evident to them, my stores being very limited ... But to save myself the daily annoyance of the creatures I at length bought it for two blankets and two shirts. Mr. Speaker, on May 9 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether, in light of the fact that he had promised residents of the Toronto region that he would cancel the Pickering airport development if more than 51 per cent of the people in metro Toronto were opposed to it, he would treat a recent public opinion poll in the Toronto Star as indicative of the feelings of the people of the region, or would he prefer to treat the opinion of the NDP on this issue in view of their switch in position in committee, as indicative of public opinion. The Prime Minister refused to answer. The words I am about to refer to were uttered in the borough of Scarborough, but they would apply to the whole of metropolitan Toronto. They were spoken on March 25, 1972, and are as follows-that if the majority of people living in this area, even if only 51 per cent, did not want this airport, the government would not proceed with it.
June 5, 1973

There have always been a great many people in the Toronto region who have questioned the need for a second airport. It was a major issue, in the election campaign in the Toronto region, of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who went on record as early as September 30, 1972, as saying that the case for a second Toronto airport had not been made. Fourteen of the 22 successful candidates in the metro Toronto region who ran in the October 30 election were on record during the election campaign as saying that there was no proven need for a second airport. Yet still the government pushed ahead, convinced that the public was still behind them on this.
Then some of the municipal councils got into the act, namely, Toronto city council representing 700,000 people, the regional municipality of York representing 166,000 people, and the township of Pickering representing 30,000 people. The councils of all these municipalities expressed opposition to the airport proceeding as planned. Yet the government still persisted. Then the Swackhammer report was completed early in January of this year, indicating that there were weighty technical arguments against the airport proceeding. As well, there was further evidence of widespread public opposition. Yet the government charged blindly ahead and on January 30 confirmed the expropriation notices on some 18,000 acres of land even though there has not been an independent inquiry to allow full public participation on the question of the need and site of the location.
That was over four months ago, Mr. Speaker. We are still waiting for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to announce the terms of reference and membership of the independent inquiry, notwithstanding that he originally promised that it would be reporting within one year of his January 30 announcement. We are anxiously awaiting that announcement and I hope it will be made very shortly.
As for public opinion, there was further evidence brought to the attention of the government on April 28 of this year when the Toronto Star published the result of a poll carried out by Canadian Facts Company Ltd. during the first ten days of April. This poll was conducted on a number of national and local issues and included a sample of 407 eligible voters across metro Toronto. The poll concluded with this question: Are you in favour of the proposed new airport scheduled to be built in Pickering township, or are you against it?
The result in metropolitan Toronto was as follows: 56 per cent of the people were against the airport, only 26 per cent said they were in favour, and 18 per cent said they were not sure. In the city of Toronto, which contains the riding of St. Paul's which I represent, the result was as follows: 62 per cent were against the airport, 19 per cent were in favour of it, and 19 per cent were not sure. Mr. Adjournment Debate
Speaker, over three to one were against it in the city, and if you take the entire metropolitan region, over two to one were against the airport.
Is it not about time to say to the Prime Minister: How about it? Will you honour your word to the people of the metropolitan Toronto region? Will the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport continue to ignore the facts which I have stated, or will the government continue to push blindly ahead, bolstered by the votes in committee of NDP members who in a moment of utter hypocrisy voted on estimates to give the government the money to push ahead with this unnecessary project? The whole project at Pickering runs counter to the environmental, economic and human needs of the urban region of metropolitan Toronto. When will this government begin to listen to the people?

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time because today, June 6, marks the twenty-ninth anniversary of D-Day, and I am sure I speak for all members of the House and all Canadians in requesting a moment to pay homage to those valiant soldiers who took part in the allied invasion of Normandy.
Canadian veterans who took part will reflect today, I am sure, wherever they may be, on events which took place on the beaches of France some 29 years ago and think of their comrades who fell by their side and were denied the chance to return to Canada to avail themselves of the great opportunities of our growing and prosperous country. At a time when there is such a great amount of technology, much of life is rather impersonal and I have always appreciated the personal approach taken by those who are employed by the postal department.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I think what the hon. member for Calgary North has said indicates he is attempting to amend the National Housing Act by amending this particular amending bill. It is a well known principle of the House of Commons that one cannot do that, more particularly when one is dealing with a supply bill which would give the government of the day authorization to expend money. The citation from Beauchesne read by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is to the point I believe. I will repeat it for the edification of hon. members. It is citation 398 which reads:
... though no amendment can be moved to the granting or enacting words of Bills for granting aids or supplies to the Crown, or to the enacting words of other Bills. Those words are part of the framework of the Bill and are never submitted to the committee.
It seems to me this is a bill granting supply to the Crown, and that this is an attempt to go beyond the limits of the amendment by going to the heart of the act itself. As such, I submit that the motion should be ruled out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I raise a point of order concerning the point of order raised by the minister. I submit to you that the chairman of the committee erred in making the particular ruling alluded to by the minister. Of course, that is not the first time that a committee chairman has made a mistake in ruling. The purpose of section 59 is to make a slight amendment to the act as it now stands. The act now provides that loans can be made to an Indian for the construction of a home. The bill seeks to expand that by providing that loans may be made to Indians for the purchase, renovation or construction of homes on Indian reserves, and defines Indians as that class of people mentioned in the Indian Aet.
National Housing Act
I submit that the amendment seeks to say, and I think I can anticipate the feeling of members who wanted this amendment brought forward, that the provisions of the law which are now confined to Indians as defined in the Indian Act, and particularly Indians on Indian reserves, shall be expanded and encompass Indian people who may not be defined in the act. I submit that we may find it impossible to define an Indian for general classification purposes, because it would be presumptuous on the part of this parliament to make that determination. The amendment seeks to establish that Indians, without the status of Indians under the act, shall be permitted to apply for loans that are available to those people on the reserves. The amendment would apply also to Indian people with respect to the purchase, construction or renovation of housing. I see the minister shakes his head. I realize that it is easy for him to be negative.
I submit that the amendment seeks to do just what I suggest, to extend the application of these loans. That, I submit, would come within the ambit of the royal recommendation. The provisions of the law in this regard would then apply to Indian people who live off the reserve, to those Indian people who are not narrowly defined under the Indian Act. After all, it would be a one-sided obligation on the part of this parliament if it were to try to determine who is or who is not an Indian, or who has or who does not have the status of an Indian, as the case may be. The amendment must be worded in this way. It would apply to individuals who are Indians but who do not have status under the Indian Act, and to incorporated groups, such as the Metis Association, the B.C. Association of non-status Indians or the Yansi group of Indians in the Yukon. It would include any other group of Indian people which is excluded by the definition in the Indian Act. That is what the amendment seeks to do. In short, it seeks to provide that the law that applies in some respects to Indians who are on the reserve shall apply also to Indians who do not live on the reserve, and shall apply without distinction. I submit that the amendment is in order, Mr. Speaker, on that basis.

Mr. Speaker, I can hardly add anything further to the reply given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in answer to the question asked by my hon. colleague.
Indeed, the bank credit expansion rate continues to be very high, and one can hardly expect the government to move towards a restrictive monetary policy. The monetary policy continues to be expansionist, and the credit supply meets the real needs of the economy. Moreover, the Minister of Finance has made a firm commitment to maintain an adequate rate of expansion of the money in circulation, that is, a rate compatible with strong and sustained growth in the production and employment sectors. From this viewpoint, the recent increases in interest rates have been a necessary response to the marked increase in foreign interest rates. Moreover, the heavy demand for credit resulting from a very rapid economic growth has, of course, exerted pressures on interest rates. We may note, however, that short-term rates of interest in Canada fell, early in the year, to much lower levels than comparable rates abroad, and that the Canadian rates are still low when compared with those abroad. It is therefore incorrect to suggest that the recent hike in interest rates reflects a move towards a restrictive monetary policy.
The monetary policy as reflected in the growth of the total amount of money in circulation and in credit conditions in general, is intended to contain any excessive increase in bank credit. The rate of expansion of this bank credit is still high. Bank loans in general have gone up by more than 20 per cent over the twelve-month period ending in May of this year. Since January, these loans have increased at a real rate of approximately 35 per cent. Consumer loans have increased somewhat more rapidly than loans to enterprises, but it is still true that, whatever measure is passed, the expansion of bank credit has been very strong.
It is clear that this very rapid expansion of bank loans must be adjusted downward, at a bearable rate. In Canada as in other countries, slowing down the rate of increase in bank credit sometimes tends to affect more particularly the small enterprises or the less favoured regions of a
Adjournment Debate
country. Now, as the Minister of Finance noted in his answer to my hon. colleague, measures have been adopted to ensure that this adjustment does not lay an undue burden on unfavoured regions or small enterprises in general.
Indeed, the minister and the Governor of the Bank of Canada asked chartered banks to pay particular attention to the needs of small enterprises and poorer regions, and the minister has declared himself satisfied with the favourable reaction of the banks. The Governor of the Bank of Canada is in close communication with chartered banks concerning their practice in granting loans, and the situation is being controlled each day. For the time being, the government is convinced that the chartered banks are doing everything possible to ensure an adequate money supply in those sectors.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will say that it is clearly in the interest of Canadians of all areas of the country to avoid an excessive credit increase. An expansion of credit beyond what is necessary to sustain a strong economic growth would contribute to the inflationary pressures and risk to end in a situation where everyone would be a loser.

June 12, 1973
Adjournment Debate
A second related question that I should like to put to the minister is: Where will the National Energy Board acquire the competence to make the kind of judgments which, in essence, have more to do with the national economy and with the environment in the sense of ecological values than it has to do with energy? Will the studies into the rail line, the liquid natural gas line, the effects on the economy and on the ecology that are now being undertaken by interdepartmental task forces, so I am informed in answer to order paper questions, be made available to the National Energy Board for study in advance of undertaking any hearing of an application for a gas pipeline? If such information is supplied to the National Energy Board by the government, will the National Energy Board take official notice of the information obtained from such studies and cite it as evidence in support of its conclusions?
A third related question is this: If, indeed, such information is to be made available to the National Energy Board by the government, without which I fail to see how the Energy Board can be considered to have the competence to make the kind of decision the minister attributes to it, then will the information also be made available to parliament so that the elected representatives of the people of Canada will be able to pass judgment upon the decision of the National Energy Board, which in the final analysis is responsible to parliament?
My final remark is more in the way of a statement of conviction than a question. Even if we are assured that all the information and all the powers, which my questions of this evening have implied are necessary in order for the National Energy Board to make a competent decision with respect to a northern pipeline, are placed at the board's disposal, I would deny that it is right and proper that a non-elective body such as the National Energy Board, rather than parliament, should make a decision of such magnitude.
Just listen, Mr. Speaker, to what the draft report on the Evaluation of the Impact on the National Economy of a Northern Canadian Gas Pipe Line says about the economic effect of the demand for $4.5 to $5 billion of capital. At page 13 the report reads:
The construction and operation of a northern gas pipeline, even if it were to carry a substantial proportion of Canadian gas, would likely prove to be a mixed blessing to Canada.
On the following page the report reads:
During pipeline operations, the maximum benefits to Canada would be additional Canadian incomes of $366 million per year, of which government revenues would comprise $73 million, and 150 to 200 permanent jobs.
The potential costs of pipeline operations include:
(a)	a continuous upward pressure of up to $183 million per year
on the Canadian dollar, making it more difficult for other, more
labour-intensive, exports to be sold abroad; and
(b)	a potentially serious upward pressure on the level of the
Canadian energy prices.
I am not willing to have an appointed board make a decision involving implications of that magnitude. I would insist that that is a job for the representatives of the people, for the Parliament of Canada. If I may, in the few seconds remaining to me, be permitted an aside, I find it passing strange, if indeed the economic effects that I have

just put on the record do result from a huge demand for capital for the construction of a vapour state gas pipeline, that the government is not doing something to reduce the costs involved in constructing such a line. For example, I find it difficult to understand why the government feels it is not necessary to finance a test loop for a liquid natural gas pipeline in order to discover whether the potential saving of up to 50 per cent claimed for such a system is indeed realizable.
Instead of doing that, the government has said that is the responsibility of the industry. Private industry is not interested in doing that because right now gas has a seller's market and the constructing of test loops would mean a delay. Customers will absorb the additional costs in any case. If there is a saving to be made, it must first come from government action.

I will get to Canada and the Conservative party in a moment. President Nixon made it crystal clear that he was not imposing wage controls because the wage increases achieved by working people in the United States were not inflationary.
The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) who moved this motion today and who, as already has been pointed out, changed his position diametrically from what it was less than two years ago, has called for a temporary freeze on all incomes, to be followed by the working out of an incomes policy. In the few minutes at my disposal I want to look at the proposals which he made on behalf of the Conservative Party.
It is relatively easy to control or freeze wages. It is easy to know precisely what the steelworker in Hamilton, the autoworker in Windsor or Oshawa, and the railway worker in Montreal make per hour and to say that they will not be allowed to make more than 2 per cent, 3 per cent or 5 per cent above that amount in the next year. But I challenge the Conservative Party to say in detail-they have not done it today or any other day-how they would regulate and control the rest of the economy.
Let us look at the things you would have to control if you really are talking about an incomes policy and an equitable distribution of restraint on all sectors of the economy. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) talked about the wage-price spiral. I am not going to say that wages do not have an effect on prices, and the hon. member for Trinity was extremely careful not to say a word about increased profits. So, Mr. Speaker, because hon. members know that I am somewhat biased, let us just turn to the record as it appears in recent issues of the Globe and Mail in the financial pages.
On June 9, 1973, the Globe and Mail carried a story which reported that for the first quarter of 1973, corporation profits were up 53 per cent over the same three months in 1972. That is the biggest quarterly advance in 12 years. On May 1, 1973, the Globe and Mail reported that Canada Packers' profits were up from $10 million the year before to $14 million for the same period this year. On April 19, the Globe and Mail reported that for the first quarter of 1973, International Nickel's profit had risen to $36 million from $1814 million in the same period in 1972, an increase of almost 100 per cent. On May 1, the Globe and Mail reported that Ford Motor Company had a record first quarter profit of $37.6 million, compared to $23.2 million in the first quarter of 1972. On April 27-I pass this along to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander)-the Globe and Mail reported that Dofasco profits had increased to $11,800,000 for the first quarter of 1973, from $8,200,000 for the first quarter of 1972.

Indeed, every person who has taxable income in Canada will benefit by the changes contained in this bill.

This provision will not only reduce income tax; it will also concentrate the reduction where there is greater need for it, that is for the small or medium wage earner.

June 21, 1973
Wheat Sales
the grains group, Rod Bryden, started to appear in Winnipeg more and more. They held a meeting every Monday. Finally the minister and his officials panicked. Orders were passed down from on high, to use the minister's words, to dispose of the grain.
We all know what happened in 1970. Our grain was fire-saled around the world. It was common knowledge in the grain trade in those days that the Canadian Wheat Board did not have the right to make a decision. That is another reason this resolution is before the House today. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board ordered a reduction in commercial stocks of some 200 million bushels without any compensation to the producers. This is what led to the five consecutive drops in farm deliveries. The minister purposely set about scaring the pants off western farmers. Change and confusion reigned supreme. All he did was stir the pot.
Virtually nothing was done overseas to promote markets. That is where the real changes were. There were quota changes, boxcar allocation changes, a block system was set up, a rapeseed committee, the whole works. It was not until disaster struck in eastern Europe and Asia that western farmers were bailed out of their difficulties-no thanks to the minister and the grains group. All they proved was that Canada could give away her grain.
I wish to quote Mr. A. M. Runciman, president of United Grain Growers. He is probably one of the most respected men in the grain business in Canada. He was commenting on the conclusion in the Canadian Wheat Board report and said:
One cannot criticize the Canadian Wheat Board for selling the grain offered it by farmers at the best competitive prices. It is the board's job to sell grain and the government's to create policies and programs that will enhance farmers' incomes. . . . And we could be highly critical of a government that, outside of its $68 million "two-price wheat" program, provided little in the way of income support to prairie grain growers.
A turmoil of farm policies, muddied by political rhetoric and conflicting views of farm organizations, carried over from the previous year. A National Farm Products Marketing Council was finally established and this inward-looking legislation was accompanied by conflicting government publicity-
He made reference to the two-price wheat subsidy. The so-called wheat payment often went to people who never produced a bushel of grain. He said nothing was done overseas to promote the sale of our grain. There are two overseas offices, one in Tokyo and one in London. We used to have an office in the Common Market, in Brussels, but it was closed. This was the biggest slap in the face to the Common Market that Canada could have delivered. It was finally reopened last year.
The minister commented on the fact that we have 208 million bushels of wheat in storage. That was the amount on June 6. We still have seven weeks to go until the end of the crop year, at which time the minister said there will be 100 million bushels available. The new crop will not start coming in until around October 1. From my vantage point, this makes the picture look a little desperate.
The minister likes to compare Canadian wheat prices with American wheat prices. That is like comparing apples with oranges. You cannot compare Canadian wheat with American wheat, and the minister knows it. I remember when France started dumping grain on the world market

in 1962. The Wheat Board received some real direction from the government. They were ordered not to match the French price cuts. The Americans agreed to go along with that. We held back. The result was that in the next year we had record sales and record high prices. This is the type of direction the Canadian Wheat Board needs. We have had nothing but stopgap measures, when what we need is national programs. The minister was nothing more than a front man for a bunch of civil servants.
Some mention was made of the 2,000 hopper cars. Over the last 15 years the average increase in Canadian grain exports has been less than 2 per cent per year. I suggest the 2,000 hopper cars are welcome, but I still say they were purchased for political reasons. I should like to think that the Canadian Wheat Board is now doing all right, that it is coming out of its slump along with the minister. The theory of supply-management appeared along with the Lift program in 1976, with the marketing bill in 1970-71, with the stabilization bill of 1971 and the adjustment program of the same year. Members of the NDP and the Eiberal Party were in support of the principles of those four programs. I believe in supply-management, but I believe in it at the farm or ranch gate where decisions can be made by 250,000 farmers rather than by a handful of bureaucrats.

Mr. Speaker, I will be as brief as I can. I simply want to say this is one of the few occasions in my almost eight years in parliament that I have felt such a deep spirit of co-operation among all parties to get on with solutions to one of the serious problems in this country. From my personal experience, having been directly involved, I was gratified to see the degree of support this bill appears to have, at least at this stage. Whenever I get in this mood, of course, I always fear the gods will descend and prove that one has to be immediately humbled. With the various things with which I am trying to cope, I am sure that will happen before too long, but I hope not in this area.
I want to deal with one or two items. First, I must admit to having noted a possible misinterpretation of meaning in my own remarks in Hansard which I made at the opening of the second reading debate on Wednesday. Either I did not explain myself clearly or there was an error in the printing. I refer to the first paragraph on page 4953 of Hansard. I will not bore hon. members by repeating what I said at that time; I simply want to make the point for those who wish to follow it up. I intended to indicate that the cases to be reviewed involve individuals who were in Canada prior to November 30. However, the statement which appears in Hansard indicates that they must have been awaiting the disposition of their appeal prior to November 30. That appears to exclude all persons whose

appeals were entered subsequent to November 30. That, of course, is not the case; it is not the intention. This is slightly complicated. If one reads my comment today he will understand this is my intent. I want to be very precise so there will be no possibility within human competence to get off on the wrong foot. I do not think it is a major item but I want to correct it.
There have been many suggestions of a concrete nature in every speech I have listened to in this debate. As far as I can tell, the questions were quite legitimate and constructive. I will attempt to deal with these in detail and any others that arise when we get to committee, hopefully fairly soon. There is one other question of statistics that might be useful to correct now. The hon. member for York East (Mr. Arrol) mentioned the difficulties in connection with the new regulations issued in January and quoted a number of people who reported under the requirement for non-immigrants to register if they stayed over 90 days, and if they wished to work to apply for employment visas. At an earlier stage I had mentioned a figure of under 10,000. I was concerned about the rate of registration taking place at that time.
So that the record is clear-and I am sure the hon. member got this figure from my remarks-on that occasion there were, finally, just under 29,000 who came forward to register because of their stay of over 90 days. We applaud that. There were just under 20,000 employment visas. So there was a total of over 48,000 people by April of this year who took cognizance of and responded to this new requirement to register.
I will be seeking the support of all hon. members as a follow-up to this debate and when the bill is proclaimed to do what hon. members have suggested, namely, act as missionaries and advocates, particularly to the ethnic groups of this country, to make it clear that we intend to be very fair. We want the people affected to take advantage of this last opportunity to get their house in order and gain the opportunity to become full Canadian citizens and contribute as so many have in the past to the growth of our society.
I will work very closely with anyone who wants to help me on this. I appreciate the offers that have been made and I intend to follow them up. There will be a large publicity campaign. All the trimmings are now being put together, particularly with regard to contacting ethnic circles, ethnic leaders and the ethnic press. I will disclose the details as they unfold when we get further into that.
I wish to express my gratitude to all members who have participated in this debate. I think probably we can now put a package together that will get us out of the woods and many people out of the woodwork when this effort is completed.

Mr. Speaker, needless to say it gives me great pleasure to speak on behalf of my party in support of the speedy passage of Bill C-202. It is good to see the minister back in his old, familiar position in the House. As he intimated in his remarks, he was formerly minister of veterans affairs and it is only too bad that the present minister, himself a veteran of very much suffering, could not be here this afternoon to see the bill passed through all stages, which I certainly hope will be the case.
I must also say that we should pay tribute to the hon. member for Edmonton West, and our House leader who has agreed to speedy passage of this bill, as well as to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe who is the official opposition critic but unfortunately is not here today; thus, it is my good fortune to be able to speak to this bill on his behalf. While paying tributes I think I should also mention the chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, the hon. member for Labelle, who has contributed to the fair-mindedness and fair play that have always been shown in the veterans affairs committee.
We want speedy passage of the bill, too, for the very reason that the minister mentioned, namely, that unless the bill receives royal assent this month the veterans will be deprived of their pensions for the months of July. Clause 3 provides:
This act shall come into force on the first day of the month immediately following the month in which this act receives royal assent.
So it is imperative that royal assent be given with all possible speed. The other reason for passing the bill is that it has taken 50 years-ever since 1918 when we first began to have veterans in our society-to do something really meaningful for the men who served their country so well in its time of need. The year 1968 was a landmark in that the Woods committee report was brought forward. The year 1972 brought the compilation of the joint study group on which this legislation is based. I suppose that this afternoon in 1973 will be a third landmark if we pass this bill to give the veterans their long awaited just desserts.
Perhaps we should not saddle the minister with blame for the delay in introducing the bill, for week after week we in this party, as well as the hop. member for Winnipeg North Centre, have questioned the minister regarding when we would have this legislation. This is another reason we welcome it greatly this afternoon.
The bill itself gives us almost everything that the joint study group asked for, as the minister mentioned. As a

matter of fact, the basic disability pension is $175 more than the joint study group asked for in their report. The percentages by which married people will receive additional benefit, those with one child and so on, are identical to the percentages recommended by the joint study group report. However, what the bill does not contain is so vital and so important that we must mention it, and that is the escalation principle which was recommended in the joint study group report.
In order to be assured that the basic pension will not again fall so far behind the standard of living of unskilled workers in the public service in the selected group of categories, the final report of the joint study group, in paragraph (i) of its recommendations, recommended:
Pension should be adjusted annually on a fixed date in accordance with changes in the average wage rates for the public service group selected and taking into account income tax deductions in effect on that fixed date-
I am a bit worried at this omission because at all stages of the study in committee of this matter everybody was so happy to think that at long last the government had accepted this new principle for establishing a basic rate rather than the old cost of living principle. Anyone studying increases in wages and salaries knows very well that the standard of living increases faster than does the cost of living. My hurried and rather cursory examination of the bill indicates there is no provision at all for any escalation. Granted that the $175 more than the study group asked for does represent an increase that will be satisfactory perhaps for one year or even two years, but beyond that are we going to allow pensions again to lag behind? This is what worries me. However, I notice that the veterans' organizations accept this bill. I suppose they feel that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, or that a crumb is better than no bread at all.
As has been said in the House, we should give the bill speedy passage, and we are now in committee of the whole in order to do this. The only other thing that annoys me and other members on this side of the House is that the two big carrots that are held out in the bill prevent us from moving amendments and trying to put in it an escalator clause which is sorely needed. If we did not do what we are doing this afternoon, we would be denying the veterans a pension increase for July and also, in effect, denying them a $175 greater basic pension than was recommended by the joint study group.
For these two reasons it looks as though we are being blackmailed a little into passing a bill which should have another very important clause in it. I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs will keep this in mind and that after one year or two years have passed will introduce further legislation that includes this very important principle.

Mr. Chairman, I had not planned to contribute to the debate this afternoon. However, after considering some of the arguments made in support of this economically and socially irresponsible measure of the government, I thought it would be useful to say a few words.
The case for a corporate tax reduction rests exclusively on an argument that says by making such a reduction we can guarantee an increase in employment. This is quite apart from the question of equity or sharing the tax burden between individuals and the corporate sector of Canada. That is another argument which would not at all justify a reduction in taxes for the corporate sector.
The real point has to be made. It is said that by cutting back 9 per cent of the corporate tax, somehow we are going to create more employment for the people of Canada. There is not one authority or one economist, in Canada or outside who would be able to present to his professional colleagues in economics an argument that could draw a

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
causal connection between this kind of tax reduction and job creation. Why not? The answer is simple. In our kind of economy, if you have a potential for expanding, selling goods and making a profit, you are going to move in that direction. You are going to expand in any case. If you are offered a chance by this government to reap greater profits, with no assurance that you are going to sell your goods, why would you expand sell or hire more employees just to have your goods pile up in storage and go unsold? You would not do that: it is palpably obvious that you would not do it. You would produce exactly the way you intended to produce, quite apart from the tax reduction, and reap the great benefit of tax gain provided by this measure. You would reap, in a year when profits in the corporate sector are at almost unprecedented levels, even higher profits. The argument in support of a corporate tax reduction- which has to be job creation-has not and cannot be made.
Any reason for supporting this measure is lacking. Any member of parliament who wants to consider the question of taxation, the fairness of the tax burden and the fact that 20 per cent of our population lives at or below the poverty line, a very large percentage of who pay taxes, must oppose this bill. If it cannot be justified in terms of job creation, it certainly cannot be justified in terms of sharing the tax burden among the various sectors of the Canadian economy.
I know I speak in vain when I urge the members of the Conservative Party to reconsider this bill and oppose the government. I know there is nothing better than this bill to reveal their corporate souls. If they are interested in having an election, nothing could be better in terms of squarely facing the issue of what kind of society we want to develop than the issue of the tax burden in this country. If they would support us on this and oppose the government, they would get a lot of support from the ordinary people of Canada, if not a high degree of exuberance on Bay Street in Toronto.
The government is abandoning the progressive methods it revealed within the first three months of this parliament by bringing in increases in pensions, reductions in taxes for lower income people and improved housing legislation. It is abandoning that initial, positive, progressive thrust by bringing in these corporate tax proposals. I hope it will not continue in this direction. Unless it continues to rely, literally and politically, on the people to my right for support, it will not continue in office with this type of legislation.

Speech:
Mr. Chairman, let us deal with the problems of the small manufacturer. All the corporation's active business income for purposes of taxation will be treated as manufacturing and processing profits if that corporation meets all the following tests. First, its active business income together with that of any other Canadian corporation with which it associates is $50,000 or less. That is the current qualification for the small business rate of taxation which at present is 25 per cent and which will be 20 per cent under the proposal before the committee.
Second, its gross revenue from the sale of goods which it manufactures or processes in Canada-and where custom

processing is involved we take the gross revenue for manufacturing or processing in Canada of goods for sale or lease by another person; in other words, we are considering here a custom processor-is greater than 75 per cent of its total gross revenue from all active business that it carries on. In other words, if the manufacturing or processing component is at least 75 per cent, there is no problem with allocation.
Third, it is not engaged in any of the activities specifically excluded from manufacturing and processing in subparagraphs (i) to (ix) of proposed section 125.1(3) (b), which is now before the committee.
And fourth, it does not carry on any foreign active business.
If it meets these qualifications, and if it can establish that its gross revenue from the sale of goods which it manufactured and processed in Canada is 75 per cent of its total income, there is no problem with allocation. There is no need to allocate beyond that.
What of businesses that do not qualify for the small business rate? The formula puts together two allocations in order to establish the amount of income that will qualify for the reduced rate. First, it looks at the total manpower bill and the portion of that bill devoted to manufacturing activity. Second, it looks at the total fixed capital of the corporation, and at the amount of that fixed capital utilized in its manufacturing activity. Then it places the amount of manufacturing labour and capital over the total labour and capital, and that is the proportion of the corporation's eligible business income which is taxed at the reduced rate.
That is not a difficult proposition. Most corporations can allocate the manpower requirements attached to a particular operation. They know how much their labour costs. That calculation is carried out in most businesses. It is not hard to allocate how much of your total fixed assets you are devoting to the manufacturing or the processing component of your business. These components are already isolated in the minds of most businessmen. Certainly, the treasurer or comptroller of any company will not experience any difficulty in isolating these components, because they are isolated for the purpose of keeping some control over business costs.
Clearly any business that does not know what its labour costs are or does not know what its fixed assets are and how much should be allocated to any particular operation is in trouble. That is why I am saying that this really is not a complicated process, because those two main components, labour and fixed capital, are known. Therefore, if you relate the manufacturing and processing component to the total labour and capital component, you will have a pretty good idea of how much in come you should apply with respect to this tax.

These contracts may be terminated by either side on three months written notice. Agreed charges are low-contract rates voluntarily agreed to by shippers and railways in return for which the shippers agreed to ship a stated percentage of their traffic by rail.
Shippers affected by the increases have a number of options. But there is no general increase in freight rates anticipated in the maritimes.

With reference to demurrage charges, these are tariffs designed not to produce revenue but rather to impose a penalty so as to prevent shippers from using railway cars for storage. No changes in demurrage rates are proposed and I should stress that these charges can be quite flexible in special cases.

Once the motion has been tabled and, according to the rules, taken up, the debate must continue without interruption, outside of routine business, for three sitting days and then a decision taken. If the measure carries, the minister must bring in a bill without delay reflecting the intent of the motion. The bill will be immediately taken up the day after it is brought before the House. By the end of seven sitting days, all the stages of the bill shall have been considered, this also without interruption, if necessary.
The purport of the amendment is to make the review procedure more meaningful. Somewhere along the line there may be something that is still uncertain. Having considered the matter, we will have put what we want to the minister in order that the review procedure will be authoritative and meaningful. We will just have to see how this gets along. It may be that all of us will be surprised.
