I am convinced that the rules of this House of Commons are making it very difficult for members to carry out their duties. We are constantly reminded of the fact there are too many supplementaries. There are not too many supple-mentaries. The problem is that we are confined to a 40 minute question period. Consequently, members feel guilty for pursuing a matter because it prohibits their colleagues from asking questions. It is necessary to pursue many questions in detail in order to keep the government on its toes. This is the responsibility of the opposition. We are cut off in the middle of our pursuit because of the 40 minute limitation.
I see no reason why it should take several months to make some minor adjustments to the rules regarding the question period. I am firmly convinced that if the question period were extended, members would find their own level of responsibility. After a few weeks, once the momentum of their questions died down, there would not be this problem with the question period. For almost 100 years there was no time limit on the question period. We must assume that for almost 100 years members of parliament were responsible, but for the past four years members have been denied the justice they deserve under the most important rules of this House. I feel guilty every time I try to ask a question. I know that by doing so, my colleagues may be denied the opportunity because of the 40 minute limit.
As things now stand, we could go on from twelve o'clock until five this afternoon killing time for most of the day with only 15 or 20 members in the House, often not even a quorum, without anyone in the country knowing what is going on. Yet this most important aspect of the work of the House of Commons, holding the government accountable for its actions, is cut off after 40 minutes. I should like to think I am speaking for all members, including members of the government party, when I say we can wait no longer for the results of the long drawn-out process of considering this matter in the committee on procedure. I think the House leaders, with some feeling that members are being gypped, must get their heads together, perhaps accept an interim report from the committee and bring about an immediate change in the rules.

Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension difficulties without necessarily at this time postponing indefinitely, or for at least 18 months or longer, the certainty of three new seats for the province of British Columbia. My riding stands to be changed very substantially as a result of redistribution and, in consequence, I will be losing part of the neighbourhood in which I grew up. I will be losing from my riding a substantial part of Vancouver South where I have campaigned, not just in the one election when I was fortunate enough to be successful in that I was elected, but as well in the previous election. Therefore, I will be losing, as I think other hon. members will, a substantial area because of redistribution and the support of people I have, hopefully, represented with diligence during the last half a year or so. This will create problems because one might always expect or hope that these people will be supporters in another election.
From a personal point of view, everything would impel me to vote for this bill. I think my fundamental duty, coming from the province of British Columbia-which ought to have an increase in the number of seats-is to keep the interests of my province and its voters in mind, and that must overrule any particular preference I might have.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard a lot of argument in this House on the recommendations contained in the Darling report; we have heard a lot of argument in favour of the construction of a Canadian merchant marine. After so much has been said, I believe the time for idle chatter is over. It is time for us to start planning for a Canadian merchant marine in which we can take pride. In this way we could provide ships for Canadian seamen and employment for workers in our Canadian shipyards.
We have heard in the last few months arguments for and against the Darling report. I think this report constitutes the basic requirement for future expansion of a Canadian merchant fleet. It is, therefore, with much concern that I view this whole report and its future relationship to a Canadian deep sea merchant marine. There is no doubt that politicians in the Atlantic provinces are opposed to this report on the ground that rail and water transportation rates will increase and that the economy of the Mari-times will be jeopardized as a result of such an increase. I do not buy that argument. I think there are other economic factors that must be considered in light of this report and in light of what we should be dealing with now and in the future. We have all heard of the Darling report and how Canadian ships should be allowed to ply between Canadian ports. We have heard about the resources in the Arctic and the offshore areas which in future will require the services of Canadian ships. We have listened to these and other arguments as to what should be done.
Another area about which I am concerned is the development of a Canadian shipping fleet. There is no justification in the argument that corporations such as IBM, Crown Zellerbach and others have been established, to the tune of millions of dollars, when B.C. shipyards are in need of work and help is not forthcoming. Surely British Columbia, with its high unemployment rate, requires some consideration when it comes to shipbuilding.
We have seen how the shipyards in eastern Canada have proven themselves very efficient and capable and will no doubt prove themselves capable of building more ships in the future, particularly if we pursue this policy in relation
Canadian Merchant Marine
to a Canadian deep sea merchant fleet. We have been shortsighted in the past with regard to these needs. Previous governments could have helped toward the retention of a fleet such as we had during the Second World War, but they have been very shortsighted and have given in to the interests of companies such as the Canadian Pacific, Irving of the maritimes and others who feel they can develop more through their own interests. Where the interests of people are concerned, surely Canadian interests are more important than the interests of these companies. It is time we got away from this kind of smokescreen.
We have seen how dummy corporations are set up to serve these private interests at the expense of the people of Canada. It is time the government took a dim view of the activities of these dummy corporations and did something more practical and justifiable in order that we might develop a merchant marine of which we can be proud. The merchant marine has helped a great deal toward the development of this country. We should reinstate this service in order that the young people of Canada can serve in it and see the world. They could then be part of the economic development of this vast sector of our economy.
We must be longsighted with regard to areas such as the Arctic and offshore development. We must be longsighted in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer. We have to institute a policy whereby the merchant marine can be developed. We must develop a policy through which it will be economically feasible to develop a deep sea merchant marine to serve the interests of this country. It is to this end that I have spoken on a number of occasions in this House in support of the Darling report. If we are to develop a deep sea merchant marine we must develop a policy along the lines recommended in that report. This must be an initial step.
A merchant marine along the lines I envisage will, I believe, soon become a reality. It must become a reality. But it requires interest on the part of the Canadian people and the Canadian government. I look forward to the expansion of our shipbuilding industry on the west coast and on the east coast. I look forward to increased employment in the shipping industry and other industries directly and indirectly associated with it. I have no doubt that this will become a reality, because water transportation is vital.
I therefore urge the federal government to make its position known in respect of the Darling report and to carry out an immediate study for the development of a merchant marine by the establishment of a Crown corporation to initiate such development. The government's interest in the matter is absolutely essential, and steps taken to boost this country's economy must be reflected in this interest. Only by being realistic about the needs of a growing economy and by following Australia's recent action to reserve the coastal shipping trade for Australia- building and manning vessels-can this country put itself in a more favourable position for a future thrust in the deep sea trade.

July 9, 1973
Canadian Merchant Marine

Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 18, as recorded in Hansard at page 4840, I put a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) as follows:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the discussions that took place earlier in this session, but which were never finalized, concerning the possibility of lowering the pensionable age under the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to age 60, will the minister before the end of this session be making a statement on this matter?
The minister's reply was given to me in a very friendly manner but, even so, the answer was no. I then put a supplementary question to the minister asking if he would give consideration to the question of lowering the pensionable age as a priority measure during the lifetime of this parliament. The minister answered that he had been prepared to discuss the matter when his estimates were before the standing committee but that the standing committee chose otherwise. He concluded his reply with this sentence as found at page 4841 of Hansard:
This question is one that is being considered with all the other issues concerning the review of social security that is taking place with the provinces at the present time.
I have no doubt that it is because of that sentence that the parliamentary secretary, in preparing to make a reply tonight, has brought with him that orange book which of course outlines all of the matters in the field of social security that are now under discussion.

I raise this issue tonight not because I have anything new to say. It is simply a plain ordinary fact that the time has come for the eligible age for pensions under both the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to be lowered to age 60.1 believe that the people of Canada want and are ready for this kind of change to be made. They are prepared that it be done on a voluntary basis-in other words that such pensions shall be paid to those persons who are prepared to withdraw from the labour market. But I am convinced that the people of Canada want action in this field.
What concerns me very much is that in the earlier part of this session, during the time the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne was being debated and we were anticipating and waiting for the legislation respecting old age pensions, a great deal was said about this matter. It was said not just by some of us in this corner of the House but by hon. members to my right from the Progressive Conservative Party, and by many Liberal members sitting on the government side of the House. They urged that the pensionable age be lowered. If it could not be done for everyone they urged that it be done for spouses of pensioners or they urged that the age be brought down from age 65 to 64, to 63, to 62, to 61 and to 60.
I am sure that all hon. members will confirm that during those first couple of months of this session a great deal was said on this issue. But once the debate on the Speech from the Throne was over, and once the Old Age Security Act amendments had been brought in raising the basic pension to $100 a month and raising the amount of the supplement, very little continued to be said on this issue, except by a few of us who will not let it be forgotten.
I am concerned that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and his colleagues in the government may now think it is a quiet issue and that they do not need to be worried about it. I tell the minister, I tell the government, and I tell my good friend from St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) who is applauding what I am saying, that this issue will not die down. When the next election campaign comes along one of the questions that will be asked of members of all parties is this: "Why didn't you bring down the eligible age for pensions to age 60?"
It is nice to know that there are discussions on this question between the federal government and the provinces. It is nice to know that there are references to the lowering of the eligible age in that orange book entitled "A Working Paper on Social Security in Canada". But things that are the subject of discussion, things that get into white papers, working papers, white books and green books, have a way of surviving for a long time. I still have in my files a copy of the 1919 Liberal convention program and platform and I am still waiting for some of those 1919 proposals to be implemented.
What we want is not just discussion about this matter, not just the assurance that something will be done some day, that it is being considered along with all the other issues. We want the government to realize that in the seventies the people of Canada believe that the time has come for pensions to be made available at age 60, and we want action on this at an early date. We want it now.
July 9, 1973
